papers.abstract: Desmoplastic small round cell tumors (DSRCT) are exceptionally rare and aggressive sarcomas with limited therapeutic options and scarce clinical evidence. We aimed to characterize the clinical course and treatment of patients with molecularly confirmed DSRCT and to investigate HER2 expression as a potential therapeutic target, including real-world experience with trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). We retrospectively analyzed patients with DSRCT treated at our specialized and certified sarcoma center. Diagnosis was confirmed by detection of the pathognomonic EWSR1::WT1 fusion. Clinical characteristics, treatment strategies, surgical outcomes, HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) results were assessed. Clinical outcomes of patients receiving T-DXd were reviewed. Eleven patients were identified (median age 22 years, range 5-63; 81.8% male). HER2 IHC was 0 in three patients (27.3%), 1 + in three (27.3%), and 2 + in five (45.5%); none showed 3 + expression, and all tumors were FISH-negative. Two extensively pretreated patients with HER2 IHC 2+/FISH-negative tumors received off-label treatment with T-DXd and demonstrated initial radiological responses. One patient experienced subsequent progression and died, whereas the second maintained disease control after more than 10 cycles despite chronic dialysis and without substantial additional toxicity. This molecularly confirmed cohort highlights the aggressive clinical course and substantial unmet therapeutic need in DSRCT. HER2 protein expression was observed in a considerable proportion of tumors despite the absence of HER2 amplification. Responses to T-DXd in two HER2 IHC 2+/FISH-negative patients provide a hypothesis-generating clinical signal supporting further investigation of HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugates in DSRCT.

papers.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is increasingly recognized as a proinflammatory driver of adverse outcomes in solid tumors. Tumor-infiltrating immune cells with CH (TI-CH) actively promote tumor growth and those harboring TI-CH experience significantly worse survival. We investigated the prevalence and impact of CH on outcomes in patients with treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Peripheral blood from 125 patients with metastatic PDAC enrolled in the PASS-01 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04469556) was evaluated. CH was defined as the presence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of ≥1% in a 23 gene panel. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. CH was detected in 36.8% (46 of 125) of patients, and DNMT3A (60.9%) and TET2 (17.4%) were the most frequently mutated genes. There was no significant difference in progression-free survival (PFS; median, 4.9 v 5.2 months; HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.68 to 1.49]; P = .95) and overall survival (OS; median, 9.4 v 9.6 months; HR, 0.99 [95% CI, 0.63 to 1.53]; P = .95) between CH-positive and CH-negative patients, respectively. Among patients with basal-like subtype (n = 23), the presence of CH was associated with a numerically shorter PFS (median, 2.4 v 4.7 months; HR, 2.50 [95% CI, 0.93 to 6.84]; P = .06) and OS (median, 6.2 v 10.2 months; HR, 1.37 [95% CI, 0.51 to 3.69]; P = .52). In contrast, classical subtype showed no significant differences in survival outcomes by CH. CH is prevalent in metastatic PDAC but not independently prognostic. Further examination of CH in basal subtype tumors and the role of TI-CH in PDAC is needed.

papers.abstract: Lynch syndrome (LS), caused by pathogenic germline variants (PGVs) in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, confers increased risks of colorectal, endometrial, and extracolonic malignancies. Urothelial carcinoma (UC) contributes substantially to LS-associated morbidity and mortality. We assessed its frequency, clinical presentation, genotype-associated risk, and molecular features. We retrospectively analyzed genetically confirmed adult LS carriers in the nationwide German Consortium for Familial Intestinal Cancer registry. UC diagnoses identified by International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes C65-C68 underwent manual clinical and pathologic validation. Available tumors underwent centralized pathologic review, MMR immunohistochemistry, and microsatellite instability (MSI) testing. Among 3,274 LS carriers, 144 (4.4%) had 224 primary UCs. The median age at first UC was 55 years (range, 22-79 years), and UC was the first malignancy in 50 patients (34.7%). Of 202 tumors with known location, 114 (56.4%) arose in the upper urinary tract. Metachronous and synchronous primary UCs occurred in 23 patients (16.0%) and five patients (3.5%), respectively. MSH2-associated PGVs were present in 111 patients (77.1%). In multivariable analysis, MSH2/EPCAM carrier status was associated with UC risk (hazard ratio, 4.43 [95% CI, 2.85 to 6.89]), whereas previous colorectal cancer and UC family history were not. Among 109 patients with diagnostic information, 26 (23.9%) presented with urinary tract-related symptoms, 20 (18.3%) were diagnosed incidentally, and 11 (10.1%) were diagnosed during urologic or oncologic surveillance. Of 31 lesions from 18 patients, 29 (93.6%) were mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) and 30 (96.8%) were MSI-high; all patients had at least one dMMR tumor and at least one MSI-high tumor. UC in LS occurs relatively early, is strongly associated with MSH2/EPCAM carrier status, and represents the first malignancy in one third of patients. These findings support prospective evaluation of genotype-adapted surveillance.

papers.abstract: The delivery of nucleic acids using nonviral vectors represents a promising approach for cancer therapy. Nevertheless, nucleic acid-based drugs suffer from poor potency and rapid degradation. Herein, we report a carrier-free nucleic acid delivery system termed Arg-CpG, which is easily constructed through charge-driven assembly of poly(l-arginine) (Arg) and the immune adjuvant unmethylated cytosine-phosphate-guanine oligonucleotide (CpG). This Arg-CpG functions as both a carrier and a therapeutic agent, thereby eliminating the need for a conventional drug delivery vehicle and minimizing potential toxicity. The guanidinium groups of Arg endow Arg-CpG with dual functionalities: enhancing cellular uptake and serving as the nitrogen donor for iNOS-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation. This NO production further synergizes with CpG to drive macrophage reprogramming toward an antitumor phenotype. Notably, Arg-CpG exhibits cell-type-dependent modulation of autophagy. It disrupts autophagic machinery in 4T1 tumor cells while preserving functional autophagy in RAW264.7 macrophages. This differential activity results in selective killing of tumor cells without compromising the viability or function of normal immune cells. Consequently, Arg-CpG elicits a robust antitumor immune response in vivo. Moreover, the modular design of Arg-CpG enables its straightforward assembly with CpG oligonucleotides and other nucleic acid payloads (e.g., anti-miR oligonucleotides and siRNA), establishing a versatile and promising platform for nucleic acid-based cancer therapy.

papers.abstract: PRGN-3008 is a CD19 CAR T cell designed to overcome key limitations in ex vivo and in vivo CAR T manufacturing, cost, safety, and therapeutic durability. Featuring decentralized overnight manufacturing without ex vivo expansion, PRGN-3008 is engineered using a single nonviral transposon to encode CD19 CAR, membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15) for improved persistence, PD-1-targeting microRNAs to prevent exhaustion, and an inducible safety switch for controlled in vivo elimination. Safety studies showed low vector copy numbers, favorable integration profile, and efficient CAR T ablation upon safety-switch activation. The combined mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation preserved PRGN-3008 polyfunctionality and sustained cytotoxicity across repeated tumor challenges, outperforming nonarmored or singly modified CAR T cells. In xenograft models, overnight-manufactured PRGN-3008 without ex vivo expansion and activation achieved durable tumor clearance, prolonged tumor-free survival, robust antigen dependent expansion, and enrichment of memory T cell phenotypes linked to clinical durability. Notably, PRGN-3008 generated from heavily pretreated patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or lupus nephritis, maintained effector function, resisted terminal differentiation under chronic antigen exposure, and effectively depleted autoreactive B cells in a humanized mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the combination of mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation enhances the expression of genes associated with bioenergetic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, glycolysis, and glutamine utilization, thereby supporting resistance to exhaustion and sustained effector function. Collectively, these data support PRGN-3008 as a clinically translatable, scalable, and controllable CAR T with the potential to expand access to cell therapy across oncology and autoimmune indications.

papers.abstract: Sex and age have an impact on efficacy and toxicity of chemotherapy (ctx) in patients (pts) with esophagogastric adenocarcinoma (EGA). However, data are limited, as clinical trials frequently do not report sex-specific differences and older pts are often underrepresented. MATEO is an international randomized trial, confirming non-inferiority of S-1 maintenance therapy compared to continued platinum-based ctx in pts with advanced EGA without disease progression after 3 months of ctx. Toxicity pattern favored S-1 monotherapy. We conducted a post hoc exploratory analysis to assess the impact of sex and age on treatment outcomes. In the per-protocol population, 112 pts (72.7%) were male and 42 (27.3%) were female. 37.7% of pts were ≥ ​70 years. Female pts more often had distal stomach tumors (64.3%), while male pts had more esophagogastric junction tumors (76.7%). In a pooled analysis, female pts showed significantly longer progression-free survival (PFS) (median 9.9 vs. 4.3 months, HR 0.56 [95% CI 0.38-0.83], log-rank: p = 0.0033), and overall survival (OS) (median 14.4 vs. 12.2 months, HR 0.65 [95% CI 0.44-0.97], log-rank: p = 0.0348). No age-related differences in PFS and OS were observed between pts ≥ 70 years and < 70 years. In multivariate analyses, female sex, but not younger age, was associated with a trend towards improved OS. No significant sex- or age-specific differences in terms of toxicity were observed. Primary tumor location differed by sex. A trend for superior outcome in female pts was observed, whereas age did not have a significant impact on outcome.

papers.abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare tumor with poor prognosis. Precision medicine and molecularly matched treatment (MMT) represent a new opportunity in oncology. We conducted a retrospective study of patients with advanced ACC within the French ENDOCAN COMETE network from 2009 to 2022 who have been providing access to molecular profiling (MP). We investigated the benefits of the MMT strategy in terms of response according to RECIST, median progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and growth modulation index (GMI). We enrolled 78 patients with ACC who underwent MP of the primary tumor in 41 patients. Most patients had metastasis at diagnosis, with at least one GRAS criterion. P53 alteration and activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway were the most frequent genetic alterations. No mutations were found in 20.5% of patients' tumors. The microsatellite instability phenotype was present in two cases. The median OS from the date of first metastasis was 33.3 months (95% CI, 24.7 to 56.2) with most patients receiving platinum-based chemotherapy and mitotane as first-line therapy. Twelve patients were treated with MMT as a second- or third-line therapy. An objective response rate was observed in two patients with a complete response under immunotherapy. The median PFS with MMT was 2.5 months. The mean GMI was 1.02, above 1.3 in three patients (4%). Molecular alteration-based precision medicine is associated with potential antitumor benefits in a limited subset of patients with ACC.

papers.abstract: Individual patient data (IPD) from oncology trials are essential for reliable evidence synthesis but are rarely publicly available, necessitating reconstruction from published Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves. Existing reconstruction methods can be affected by digitization errors, strong uniform censoring assumptions, and the inability to recover subgroup-level pseudo-IPD when only aggregate statistics are available. We developed RESOLVE-IPD, a computational framework that combines vector-based KM extraction, censoring-informed survival reconstruction, and uncertainty-aware subgroup recovery for pseudo-IPD reconstruction and subgroup meta-analysis. RESOLVE-IPD transforms published survival data into reconstructed pseudo-IPD. The framework uses VEC-KM for vector-graphic coordinate extraction and CEN-KM to incorporate censoring marks and reported risk tables into overall-population reconstruction. To address subgroup evidence recovery, we introduced MAPLE, an algorithm that identifies an ensemble of plausible subgroup labelings consistent with reported aggregate summaries. RESOLVE-IPD enables downstream IPD-based evaluations, including subgroup meta-analyses that quantify and propagate uncertainty inherent in the reconstruction process. RESOLVE-IPD was demonstrated through subgroup meta-analyses of four trials in advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, focusing on patients with low programmed death-ligand 1 expression and patients age ≥65 years. VEC-KM and CEN-KM reconstructed overall survival pseudo-IPD that closely reproduced published KM curves and reported summary statistics. MAPLE produced plausible subgroup reconstructions consistent with reported hazard ratios and survival estimates. Uncertainty-propagating meta-analysis generated pooled survival and interval-specific hazard-ratio estimates while preserving subgroup reconstruction uncertainty. RESOLVE-IPD provides a framework for reconstructing overall and subgroup pseudo-IPD from published survival information and for propagating reconstruction uncertainty, thereby supporting more robust and transparent secondary evidence synthesis in precision oncology.

papers.abstract: Epithelial ovarian cancers (EOCs) comprise biologically distinct histotypes that arise within shared anatomical niches where tumor-stroma interactions shape tumor behavior and therapeutic response. However, most classification frameworks rely on bulk profiling that conflates epithelial and stromal contributions, limiting the understanding of crosstalk between the different compartments. Here, we performed compartment-resolved transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of matched carcinoma and stroma across clear cell (CCOC), endometrioid (ENOC), and high-grade serous ovarian cancers (HGSC). Carcinoma profiles segregated strongly by histotype, whereas stromal profiles showed minimal histotype specificity and instead resolved into four shared groups (S1-S4). The S4 subtype, marked by a desmoplastic, myofibroblast-rich program, was enriched in omental tumors and corresponded to the HGSC C1/Mesenchymal signature. This subtype largely reflected tumor-extrinsic programs and was present beyond HGSC. Compartment-resolved analyses also refined the interpretation of other molecular carcinoma subtypes and revealed distinct carcinoma-intrinsic EMT-like programs. Together, these findings define a histotype-agnostic stromal architecture across epithelial ovarian cancers, clarify the cellular basis of canonical high-grade serous molecular subtypes, and reveal carcinoma-intrinsic EMT programs. This study underscores the value of physically separating epithelial and stromal compartments before molecular analysis and position this dataset as a multi-purpose reference resource for the EOC research community.

papers.abstract: Precision oncology still faces low clinical translation rates. This is largely because two-dimensional (2D) culture systems cannot reproduce tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental stress. Here, we review the applications of 3D cancer models, including scaffold-free spheroids, patient-derived organoids (PDOs) biobanks, and microphysiological systems (MPSs), in drug resistance modeling and personalized therapy. These platforms effectively model metabolic gradients, lineage plasticity, and immunological features within the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby bridging the genotype-phenotype gap. They also capture physical immune exclusion, T cell exhaustion, and antigen presentation to facilitate the evaluation of immunotherapies. Last, we discuss key translational bottlenecks such as standardization and throughput, proposing the integration of advanced biomanufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven phenomics, and computational modeling to develop 3D cancer platforms into clinical predictive systems for optimizing precision treatment strategies.

papers.abstract: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is an established driver of aneuploidy and cell death. Here, we investigate the role of apoptosis as a barrier against CIN-driven aneuploidy in B lymphocytes. We found that impairment of their spindle assembly checkpoint via deletion of Mitotic Arrest Deficient 2-Like 1 or mutation of Monopolar Spindle 1 kinase curtails B cell survival. A CRISPR screen identified intermediates of mitochondrial apoptosis as critical, which we confirmed in vivo by overexpression of a B cell-restricted BCL2 transgene, outperforming loss of P53. Notably, cell death inhibition by BCL2 was insufficient to cause aneuploidy-driven B cell transformation, while loss of P53 strongly synergized with tumors featuring stochastic aneuploidies. In contrast, high cell death rates rapidly select for specific karyotypes, facilitating aneuploid tumor cell survival in Eμ-Myc transgenic mice. Hence, cell death inhibition fails to allow CIN-driven aneuploidies to prevail. In contrast, BCL2-regulated apoptosis selects viable aneuploid tumor karyotypes in the presence of oncogenic MYC, a notion with implications for the clinical use of BCL2-targeting therapies.

papers.abstract: Non-mutational mechanisms, including copy number alterations and transcription factor dysregulation, are critical drivers of melanoma progression. Here, we identify the transcription factor MYBL2 as a key oncogenic driver located on frequently amplified chromosome 20q. MYBL2 overexpression promoted transformation and correlated with poor survival, yet paradoxically, the transactivation function of MYBL2 was dispensable for oncogenic activity. Instead, MYBL2 acquired a non-canonical RNA-binding function enabled by the melanoma-associated RNA landscape. Through these RNA interactions, MYBL2 reshaped the chromatin landscape toward an AP-1-permissive state and promoted chromatin association of the oncogenic transcription factors MAFG and FRA1, indirectly reprogramming tumor-promoting gene networks that predict poor outcomes across multiple cancers. Importantly, a decoy RNA that disrupts the MYBL2-RNA interaction impaired MYBL2 association with MAFG and FRA1 and suppressed melanoma cell growth. These findings establish MYBL2 as an RNA-binding-dependent, 20q gain-associated driver that promotes melanoma progression through chromatin and transcriptional network remodeling.

papers.abstract: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare pharmacogenetic condition with substantial morbidity and mortality. The current gold standard for diagnosis, caffeine-halothane contracture testing (CHCT), is invasive, costly, and available only at a single centre in Canada. Genetic testing offers a less invasive alternative, but access remains inconsistent across Canadian provinces. We sought to evaluate the cost-consequences and diagnostic wait times of a genetics-first vs biopsy-first strategy for MH susceptibility. We conducted a retrospective cost-consequence analysis of 1,208 patients referred to the Canadian Malignant Hyperthermia Investigation Unit (2015-2024) with a personal or family history suggestive of MH, and their first-degree relatives. We compared the direct, indirect, and societal costs of the Ontario genetics-first approach with those of a hypothetical biopsy-first approach used in other provinces. We analyzed diagnostic timelines using Kaplan-Meier survival analyses. In the genetics-first strategy, 7.2% of probands (88/1,208) had a diagnostic variant and did not require biopsy for contracture testing, resulting in modest societal cost reduction for probands compared with the biopsy-first strategy (CAD 23.5M vs CAD 24.3M, respectively; CAD 700 saved per proband tested). The costs of cascade testing of their first-degree relatives were three-fold lower for the genetics-first strategy (CAD 3.6M vs CAD 11.3M). The median [interquartile range] time to diagnosis was 2 [1-5] months for patients with diagnostic variants, compared with 39 [22-51] months for those requiring biopsy (log-rank P < 0.001). Compared with a hypothetical biopsy-first approach, offering genetics testing as initial step to all individuals with clinical suspicion of MH susceptibility did not increase societal costs, and resulted in substantial cost savings for cascade testing of their relatives, markedly shortening time to diagnosis for individuals who harbour a diagnostic variant.

papers.abstract: Residual cancer burden (RCB) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is highly prognostic of disease-free survival in patients with high-risk early-stage breast cancer, and extensive residual disease (RCBIII) indicates treatment resistance. Identifying intrinsic pretreatment resistance may enable earlier redirection to therapies more likely to achieve pathologic complete response. We aimed to identify molecular biomarkers associated with resistance to neoadjuvant therapies, develop predictive models, and create an interactive resource. We analyzed pretreatment transcriptomic data from 987 patients with stage II to III breast cancer enrolled in the randomized, adaptive, multiarm phase II I-SPY2 trial. We applied the response-weighted elastic net algorithm (RWEN) to identify gene expression signatures associated with poor response (RCBIII) versus good response (RCB0/I). Using these gene sets, we trained random forest (RF) models to predict response and benchmarked them against models trained using randomly sampled gene sets. To evaluate robustness, RWEN-derived gene sets were evaluated in 1,127 nonoverlapping validation I-SPY2 cohorts, including independent paclitaxel control arms, paclitaxel plus immunotherapy arms, and receptor subtype-matched patient subsets. We derived resistance-associated gene sets across nine treatment arms and receptor subtypes, implicating immune evasion, chromatin remodeling, DNA repair deficiency, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) signaling. In the validation cohort, models using the paclitaxel gene set achieved sensitivity = 0.88/specificity = 0.65; models using the pembrolizumab gene set across immunotherapy-containing arms achieved sensitivity = 0.78/specificity = 0.69; models using subtype-specific gene sets achieved sensitivity = 0.61-0.71/specificity = 0.65-0.74 across hormone receptor-positive, and triple-negative gene sets. We make public ISPY_Explore which enables visualization of gene and protein expression by treatment arm, receptor subtype, and response. This integrative approach identified biologically diverse resistance-associated gene sets with predictive and translational potential. ISPY_Explore provides a cloud-based tool for exploring molecular data and may guide the development of personalized treatment strategies to overcome resistance in high-risk breast cancer.

papers.abstract: People with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) are at risk for developing peripheral nerve sheath tumors (PNSTs) ranging from benign neurofibromas to high-grade sarcomas. PNSTs known as atypical neurofibromas are at increased risk for malignant transformation. In 2017 the term ANNUBP (atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential) was proposed for PNSTs at increased risk for malignant transformation based on histopathologic features. Subsequently it was recognized that PNSTs not meeting ANNUBP criteria could still have concerning clinical, imaging and molecular features. A State of the Science conference addressed how to define these pre-cancerous PNSTs and reached consensus regarding clinical management and priority areas of research. Key recommendations from this symposium include: (1) using a combination of histologic, molecular and imaging features to define pre-malignant "at-risk" PNST; (2) recognizing that people with NF1 may be divided into "higher-risk" and "average-risk" for MPNST based on features such as their germline NF1 variant, internal tumor burden and history of malignancy or radiotherapy and; (3) the need to validate consensus screening and surveillance strategies based on personal and tumor-related risk factors. These recommendations will advance the ability to standardize care, and potentially fuel research that enables early diagnosis, prevention of malignant transformation and improved outcomes.

papers.abstract: Most studies evaluating O-(2-[18F]-fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine (FET) PET for glioblastoma progression rely on single-scan assessments, leaving diagnostic uncertainties in cases with borderline tracer uptake. We evaluated metabolic activity evolution during the transition of glioblastoma progression using serial FET PET to determine whether longitudinal parameter changes improve diagnostic certainty. Between 2016 and 2026, 182 patients with glioblastoma undergoing 690 dynamic FET PET scans (median, 3; range, 2-12) were retrospectively evaluated. Eligible cases required documented progressive disease according to RANO 2.0 criteria and serial FET PET at least 2 time points (at suspected progression and within a 6-month prior window). Static PET parameters, ie tumor-to-brain ratios (TBRmean, TBRmax) and metabolic tumor volume (MTV), and their longitudinal changes were evaluated according to PET RANO 1.0 criteria, alongside additional dynamic PET parameters (time-to-peak). Single-scan metrics and serial changes were compared in cases with borderline uptake. Ninety patients with 102 confirmed progression events met all selection criteria (median interscan interval, 2.7 months). At progression, TBRmean, TBRmax, and MTV increased significantly (P < .001). Median percentage increases were modest for TBRmean (+4%) and TBRmax (+17%), whereas MTV exhibited a substantial expansion (+182%). In cases with borderline uptake, applying a longitudinal MTV increase criterion of ≥40% per PET RANO 1.0 substantially improved progression detection to up to 89%, yielding a 14% higher diagnostic detection rate compared to single-scan thresholds. In glioblastomas with documented RANO 2.0 progression, integrating longitudinal MTV changes markedly improves diagnostic certainty over single-scan uptake metrics, particularly in challenging cases with borderline uptake.

papers.abstract: The IDH1/2 inhibitor vorasidenib demonstrated efficacy in residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant gliomas after surgery. However, there is lack of knowledge regarding factors predicting the probability of response. We conducted a prospective single-centre study on 54 grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant astrocytomas and IDH1/2-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas treated with vorasidenib. MRI response (2D and 3D) and seizure outcome were longitudinally assessed. Factors associated with response were explored using regression models. With a median follow-up of 17.5 months, vorasidenib induced progressive tumour shrinkage on MRI, with median volume reductions of - 12.2% at cycle 6, -27.8% at cycle 12, and -55.5% at cycle 18. Best volumetric response was CR in 1 patient, PR in 5, MR in 9, SD in 31 and PD in 7. The ORR (CR + PR + MR) was 28%. Eighteen patients who had focal grade 3 areas showed similar volumetric response and ORR. 9/12 (75%) patients with baseline seizures achieved ≥50% reduction or seizure freedom. MRI response correlated with early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction. Vorasidenib was generally well tolerated, with liver enzyme elevation being the main adverse event. Vorasidenib induced sustained tumour shrinkage and seizure control. Early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction were associated with MRI response.

papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. Methylation of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter is the only clinically used biomarker predicting response to alkylating agents such as temozolomide and is associated with improved survival. However, its predictive accuracy is limited by an intermediate gray zone and variability in assessment methods. To reduce overtreatment of patients, improved stratification strategies are needed, potentially through integration of additional biomarkers such as MGMT protein expression. We performed a systematic review to evaluate studies comparing the prognostic value for progression-free survival and overall survival of MGMT promoter methylation and MGMT protein expression in glioblastoma patients treated with temozolomide, including 33 independent cohorts with a total of 4,691 patients. We searched three databases up to May 2025. Risk of bias was assessed with a modified Quips tool. Methylation-specific PCR and pyrosequencing indicated stronger prognostic value than immunohistochemical assessment of MGMT protein expression with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.07 (95%CI 1.61-2.66), 2.13 (95%CI 1.64-2.75), and 1.50 (95%CI 1.26-1.79), respectively. An inverse correlation between MGMT promoter methylation and protein expression was observed in only 52% of assessed studies, suggesting that promoter methylation and protein expression may contribute independently to prognosis. Substantial variability in methylation assays and protein cut-offs underscores the need for methodological harmonization in future studies and clinical practice. Integration of MGMT protein expression with promoter methylation refines identification of primary temozolomide-resistant tumors and supports the debate of withholding temozolomide in patients unlikely to benefit.

papers.abstract: Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) are the most common malignant CNS tumor in infants, and patients suffer from low survival rates and treatment-related morbidities. These tumors frequently overexpress the pan-cancer antigen B7-H3 (CD276), which can be targeted with immunotherapy. We hypothesized that adding a B7-H3-targeting cytotoxic chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) to NK cells can enhance killing against ATRTs. We designed a library of variable affinity B7-H3-targeted CARs, which were transduced into primary healthy donor-derived NK cells. We verified B7-H3 expression in a panel of ATRT cell lines and further engineered luciferase and nuclear GFP-expressing ATRT (CHLA-04, CHLA-06, BT12, BT37) as well as a CHLA-06-derived B7-H3 knockout. We tested CAR-NK cell functionality using in vitro co-culture cytotoxicity assays. We delivered anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells intratumorally or intracerebroventricularly (ICV) to ATRT orthotopic xenografts and monitored for tumor growth and animal survival. B7-H3-targeted CAR-NK cells demonstrated target-specific cytotoxicity when compared to unmodified NK cells. Knockout of B7-H3 in target cells abolished the increased CAR-mediated target killing. When delivered intratumorally to CHLA-06 orthotopic xenograft-bearing mice, anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells eliminated tumor cells and prolonged survival. When CAR-NK cells were delivered ICV against a CNS disseminated tumor model of BT12, treated mice had significantly improved survival. Anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells effectively kill ATRTs in multiple pre-clinical in vitro and in vivo models in an antigen-specific manner. Evidence of efficacy in translationally relevant models provides support for using B7-H3-targeting CAR-NK cells in high-risk ATRT patients.

papers.abstract: Variability in how clinical trial elements are reported can hinder accurate interpretation and comparison of trial results. Here, we systematically analyzed published manuscripts of therapeutic clinical trials in myelodysplastic syndromes/neoplasms (MDS) focusing on how key data elements were reported and made recommendations on how to improve this reporting. We included peer-reviewed full text manuscripts that reported results of clinical trials in MDS and were published between January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2024. We analyzed the presence or absence of several pre-determined key reporting elements and then synthesized these data to evaluate for consistency across manuscripts. We identified substantial variability in descriptions of patient characteristics, as well as the definitions used for response criteria. For example, baseline ANC was reported in only 16% of lower-risk MDS studies and 23% of higher-risk MDS studies, while baseline bone marrow blast percentage was reported in only 55% of higher-risk MDS manuscripts. In addition, response endpoints lacked standardization, with six unique definitions of RBC transfusion independence identified in lower-risk MDS trials and seven different definitions of overall response rate identified in higher-risk MDS trials. Informed by the results of this analysis, we then performed a modified-Delphi process for members of the International Consortium for MDS (icMDS) to develop consensus-based recommendations for consistent and accurate reporting of MDS clinical trial results. We advocate that these recommendations serve as benchmarks and templates for clinical trial reporting in MDS to improve interpretability and comparison of results.

papers.abstract: Malignant ascites is a lipid-rich, immunosuppressive environment that has recently emerged as a target for locoregional bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) therapy. However, the mechanisms by which ascites, particularly its lipid components, suppress antitumour immunity and limit therapeutic efficacy remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the impact of ascites lipids on T-cell immunosuppression and assessed whether lipid modulation could enhance the efficacy of BiTE therapy. Transcriptomic profiling of T cells exposed to acellular ascites fluid revealed an enriched signature associated with cholesterol efflux and incomplete fatty acid oxidation, which are metabolic features often found in exhausted T cells. These alterations converged on a metabolically imbalanced state linked to impaired plasma membrane signalling. Meanwhile, anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated T cells showed marked lipid accumulation in ascites, which was attenuated by lipid depletion. Functionally, lipid removal was associated with enhanced TCR-associated signalling, as demonstrated by increased ZAP70 phosphorylation, and restored CD137 expression while leaving CD25 unchanged. To determine whether ascites lipids also affected BiTE efficacy, T cells were cocultured with ovarian cancer cells and an EpCAM-targeting BiTE in untreated or lipid-depleted ascites. Ascites suppressed BiTE-mediated T-cell activation and abolished tumour cell killing, whereas lipid depletion contributed to the restoration of T-cell activation, IFN-γ production and BiTE-mediated cytotoxicity. Together, these findings suggest that lipids contribute to T-cell dysfunction in ovarian cancer ascites and demonstrate that lipid depletion is associated with restored antitumour T-cell activity. Targeting this metabolic barrier may therefore provide a combination strategy to potentiate BiTE therapy in malignant ascites.

papers.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed the treatment of multiple malignancies, yet primary and acquired resistance remain major barriers to attaining durable clinical benefit. Increasing evidence indicates that immunotherapy failure rarely results from a single mechanism but instead emerges from dynamic interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Recent advances in single-cell, spatial multiomics, and longitudinal profiling have revealed the complex organization of TME-mediated resistance, which can be conceptualized within three interconnected suppressive modules: the tumor-cell-intrinsic module, myeloid-suppressive networks, and stromal barriers. The relative dominance of these modules varies across spatial niches, metastatic sites, disease stages, and treatment phases, leading to profound spatiotemporal heterogeneity and dynamic reorganization of dominant resistance axes. In this Review, we propose a spatiotemporal and systems-level framework for understanding TME-mediated immunotherapy resistance. We discuss how the tumor-cell-intrinsic module contributes to immune escape, how myeloid-suppressive networks and stromal barriers sustain and amplify immunosuppression, and how reciprocal crosstalk among these modules generates feed-forward loops that stabilize resistant states. We also review clinical strategies for remodeling the TME to increase the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches. Additionally, we discuss the opportunities and challenges associated with TME remodeling, including safety considerations, emerging biomarkers, and rational combination strategies. We propose that future TME-targeted therapies should transition from component-oriented interventions to dynamic and mechanism-matched strategies guided by dominant resistance axes. This approach aims to facilitate the development of more precise and durable cancer immunotherapies.

papers.abstract: Liquid biopsies are one of the few noninvasive procedures for probing disease at the molecular level. They represent a scalable solution to cancer detection and monitoring by capturing tumor-derived signals from circulating biomolecules such as proteins, DNA, RNA, and metabolites. However, these signals are often sparse, heterogeneous, and shaped by genetics, demographics, and comorbidities. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially with multimodal foundation models, have proven capable of extracting signals from noisy, high-dimensional data. Pretraining on large cohorts and integrating complementary modalities may improve sensitivity for tumor signals in blood, though significant clinical and infrastructural barriers remain. This review synthesizes advances in liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence and examines how their convergence can enable enhanced cancer monitoring.

papers.abstract: Third-generation tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (3G-TKIs), including olverembatinib and ponatinib, are effective in people with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) failing prior TKIs, but many subjects still have poor responses and outcomes. The broader genomic and transcriptomic features associated with 3G-TKI prognosis remain incompletely defined. We interrogated genomic and transcriptomic data from 202 subjects receiving olverembatinib or ponatinib at baseline and during therapy. In penalized multi-variable analyses, the high-burden ASXL1 p.G646Wfs*12 (ASXL1G646Wfs*12) variant emerged as the most consistent genomic feature associated with inferior responses and outcomes; additional lower-frequency variants, including RUNX1, IKZF1, PHF6, SETBP1 and GATA2 variants, were also associated with responses and/or outcomes. Longitudinal genomic analyses showed that ABL1 variants frequently decreased during 3G-TKI therapy, whereas persistent, emerging or expanding non-ABL1 variant clones were enriched in resistant subjects, suggesting a shift toward BCR::ABL1-independent clonal evolution in later-line resistance. Transcriptomic analyses identified three distinct gene expression profiles (GEPs) based clusters with different prognoses. Favorable prognosis was associated with lower leukemic stemness and more immune-active transcriptional features, whereas poor prognosis was characterized by stemness- and proliferation-dominant, immune-suppressed states. These findings identify genomic and transcriptomic features associated with 3G-TKI prognosis and provide a potential framework for molecular risk stratification in later-line CML that requires independent validation.

papers.abstract: Therapeutic options for Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) have expanded but improvements in overall-survival (OS) are difficult to interpret due to competing non-WM mortality. We conducted a large single-center retrospective study of 1020 patients with WM to evaluate survival trends. Patients were stratified by era of active WM diagnosis using a two-era model (1996-2005 and post-2006). OS did not differ significantly across eras in the overall cohort (p = 0.64). However, among patients aged <65 years at the time of active WM diagnosis, OS improved in the post-2006 era (median 18.8 vs. 14.1 years, p = 0.018). Cause-specific-survival (CSS) improved across eras, increasing from 15.6 years in 1996-2005 to 18.9 years post-2006 (p < 0.0001). Competing-risk-analysis (CRA) demonstrated a reduction in WM-related mortality over time (p < 0.001). However, excess mortality persisted, with a standardized mortality ratio (SMR) of 2.79 (p < 0.001) among patients <65 years compared with a matched U.S. population. Our findings highlight improvements in WM-specific survival, while gains in OS are observed in younger patients.

papers.abstract: The optimal reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimen for older patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHCT) remains undefined. We utilized CIBMTR registry data (2013-2022) to compare five common fludarabine-based regimens in 11,731 patients aged ≥50 years: fludarabine combined with 2 days of busulfan (FB2), melphalan 100 mg/m² (FM100), melphalan 140 mg/m² (FM140), or 2 Gy TBI with (FCT) or without (FT) cyclophosphamide. Using propensity score inverse probability weighting and Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART), we found that Fludarabine-melphalan (FM) regimens demonstrated superior long-term survival. Although FM140, FCT, and FT showed higher early mortality (≤6 months) than FB2 (P=.036), both FM100 (HR 0.79) and FM140 (HR 0.77) achieved significantly better late (> 6 months) overall survival (OS), outperforming all other regimens (P<.0001). In the 2019-2022 cohort, FM100, FM140, and FCT provided improved disease-free survival (DFS) relative to FB2. Specifically, FM100 yielded superior DFS compared to FCT (P=0.002) and FT (P=0.007). FM-based conditioning consistently resulted in lower relapse rates (P<.0001) and improved late GVHD-free/relapse-free survival. While FM regimens faced higher early non-relapse mortality (NRM), this impact did not persist beyond 6 months. BART analysis confirmed that these survival and relapse benefits remained robust across various patient comorbidities. In conclusion, FM100 and FM140 provide superior long-term survival and DFS for older patients with AML/MDS by providing potent anti-leukemic activity that offsets higher early toxicity. These findings support FM-based RIC as the preferred conditioning platform for this population, regardless of baseline comorbidities.

papers.abstract: The biomedical innovation landscape is increasingly shaped by high-growth startups, particularly "unicorns"-privately held companies valued at over $1 billion. While these entities generate significant economic value and drive digitalization and novel therapeutic development in oncology, their creation and integration into the research ecosystem remain unevenly distributed globally. Notably, Europe lacked a single medical unicorn in oncology before 2026. This study investigates the geographical distribution, financing structures, and investment focus of global oncology unicorns to understand the factors behind their success. It further aims to explore the potential of these entities to contribute to oncology research funding and to identify the critical gaps in the European startup ecosystem that prevent their emergence. We identified 21 oncology unicorns from the CB Insights database with business models clearly linked to oncology. Data on company valuation, financing stages (early, expansion, later), geographical origin, investor composition, and cumulative investment were analyzed. The 21 oncology unicorns represent a cumulative market valuation exceeding $50 billion. Geographically, 18 (86%) were founded in the United States and 3 (14%) in China, with no representation from Europe or any other region outside the US and China. Investment analysis revealed that reaching unicorn status requires substantial cumulative investment, typically exceeding $200 million per company. The investor base is dominated by US-based institutional players who form large consortia. The primary business foci attracting investment are pharmaceutical drug research services, blood and genetic testing, and the development of proprietary pharmaceutical products. A small number of individual "super-investors" have participated in multiple unicorns. Oncology unicorns generate substantial value and drive innovation. Their concentration in the US suggests systemic advantages in funding, culture, and market access. The finding that over $200 million in cumulative investment is needed to build a unicorn highlights the scale of the financing gap in Europe. However, capital availability alone does not explain the translational deficit; rather, the US advantage lies in a more coherent alignment of incentives across academia, technology transfer, investors, regulators, pharmaceutical companies, and payers. A small fraction of the wealth generated by unicorns could theoretically double oncology research funding in Europe. This analysis underscores the urgent need for strategic realignment of European innovation policy-not merely to increase funding, but to create an integrated ecosystem where translational investment is sufficiently attractive for capital to remain and compound within Europe.

papers.abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) arise from and are sustained by hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) that acquire a driver mutation. Existing therapies fail to eliminate MPN HSCs, leaving allogeneic HSC transplantation (HSCT) as the only curative option. However, allogeneic HSCT non-selectively ablates both healthy and MPN HSCs, requiring donor stem-cell replacement and risking serious toxicities and death. MPN driver mutations in calreticulin (CALRmut) generate a shared C-terminal neopeptide unique to MPN cells that must be displayed at the cell surface in complex with the thrombopoietin receptor MPL to drive oncogenic signaling. These features make CALRmut an attractive target for selective immunotherapy. However, it is unknown whether MPN HSCs consistently display surface CALRmut to enable selective elimination in vivo via CALRmut targeting. We generated hAB2, a high-affinity CALRmut-specific humanized antibody, to use as the binding domain for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells. We show that functional murine and human MPN HSCs express surface CALRmut that is reliably detected by AB2 in vitro and in vivo. We developed an MPN patient-derived tumor xenograft (PDTX) model to enable rigorous testing of human MPN HSC-directed therapies in vivo. hAB2 CAR-T cells selectively eliminate CALRmut MPN HSCs in PDTX, eradicating all detectable MPN-propagating function in serial transplantation assays, while preserving co-existing normal human and host hematopoiesis. These findings establish cell-surface CALRmut display as a therapeutically exploitable feature of MPN HSCs and support the feasibility of CALRmut-targeted, transplant-free immunotherapies with curative intent for CALRmut MPNs.

papers.abstract: Over the past decade, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has achieved durable remissions in patients with relapsed or refractory haematological malignancies. However, its broader clinical adoption remains constrained by patient-specific ex vivo manufacturing, substantial treatment-related toxicities and limited efficacy in solid tumours. In vivo CAR immunotherapy enables endogenous immune cells to be genetically reprogrammed directly within the body, bypassing leukapheresis, ex vivo expansion and individualized cell manufacturing. This Review focuses specifically on in vivo CAR immune cell engineering for cancer therapy, encompassing haematological malignancies and solid tumours; applications in non-malignant diseases, including autoimmune disorders, are outside its scope. We examine emerging technologies for generating CAR immune cells in vivo and discuss how viral vectors, non-viral nanocarriers and biomimetic delivery systems could improve the precision, scalability and controllability of cancer immunotherapy. We further highlight immune effectors beyond CAR T cells, including CAR macrophages and CAR natural killer cells, whose distinct cytotoxic, phagocytic and immunomodulatory functions may offer complementary approaches to treating solid tumours. We discuss strategies involving tumour-microenvironment remodelling, metabolic adaptation and precision genome engineering to improve immune-cell persistence, mitigate functional exhaustion, enhance tumour infiltration and limit antigen escape. Emerging clinical studies in haematological malignancies provide initial proof of concept that functional CAR cells can be generated in patients, although long-term safety, durability and reproducibility remain to be established. A central challenge is to generate these cells with sufficient cellular and spatial precision while maintaining control over their activity over time. We discuss how cell-subset-specific delivery, programmable CAR circuits, multicellular engineering, intelligent biomaterials and artificial intelligence could support the development of in vivo CAR immunotherapy as a scalable, controllable and potentially repeatable cancer treatment.

papers.abstract: While a differentiation hierarchy with leukemia-initiating stem cells (LICs) at the apex is well documented for acute myeloid leukemia, the existence of LICs and their trajectories in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) are debated. This study aims to investigate the hierarchical landscape of two B-ALL cases by combining barcoding and multiome single-cell data to unveil the differentiation architecture and temporal dynamics of leukemic differentiation at clonal and single-cell resolution in vivo. Single-cell transcriptome and AbSeq analysis of lentiviral barcoded and transplanted patient-derived B-ALL cells revealed interconnected subpopulations, which could be prospectively isolated via surface markers and exhibited distinct leukemogenicity. Barcode tracking demonstrated the ability of cells to differentiate from a source cluster into differentiated progeny. Using machine learning, we identified expression patterns predicting the differentiation potential of each barcoded cell within the immature cell compartment. To determine the dynamical properties of clones, we developed a mathematical model that simulates the development of these subpopulations from a clonally diverse stem cell compartment. The model confirmed the most likely cluster of origin, supporting our functional data, and revealed the variability in dynamical properties between clones, while largely excluding plasticity. Hence, our work demonstrates unidirectional differentiation in selected B-ALL cases.

papers.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype and is characterized by a high metastatic potential and limited treatment options. TNBC frequently metastasizes to lymphatic vessels and the presence of breast cancer cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes (LNs) is an important prognostic factor. Nevertheless, the molecular and metabolic reprogramming of TNBC-associated lymphatic vasculature remains poorly understood. A comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 44,000 endothelial cells from human breast tumor datasets was performed. RBP1, a retinol-binding protein, was identified as a metabolic gene highly and specifically upregulated in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Then, RBP1 expression in human TNBC biopsies was assessed, and its association with LN status and overall patient survival was investigated in a cohort of 1,474 breast cancer patients. We further evaluated the in vivo relevance of RBP1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout in a pre-clinical TNBC mouse model. In vitro functional studies were performed using co-culture systems and RBP1-silencing in LECs. Finally, RBP1 mechanism of action in the lymphatic vasculature was determined by bulk-RNA sequencing and validated by applying different cellular and molecular approaches. Single-cell profiling revealed that the metabolic gene RBP1 was upregulated in LECs within the human breast tumor microenvironment. Further analysis showed that lymphatic RBP1 expression was associated with LN metastases, and correlated with poor prognosis and reduced survival in TNBC patients. In the pre-clinical TNBC mouse model, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout reduced lymphangiogenesis, tumor growth and metastatic burden, and increased necrosis. Moreover, functional assays demonstrated that direct co-culture of LECs with TNBC cells, or exposure to their secretome, induced lymphatic RBP1 upregulation and enhanced pro-lymphangiogenic activities, whereas RBP1 silencing compromised their biological, redox and metabolic properties. Mechanistically, bulk RNA sequencing of RBP1-silenced LECs combined with experimental validation revealed that RBP1, through its retinol-binding domain, modulates the VEGFR3 and NOTCH pathways, while also involving lipid mobilization. We define lymphatic RBP1 as a key "switch" that couples LEC metabolism to molecular programs, thereby driving tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis, breast tumor growth and lymphatic dissemination in TNBC. Our findings underscore the potential of RBP1 as both a novel prognostic biomarker and a tractable therapeutic target for blocking TNBC progression and lymphatic metastasis.

papers.abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure certain hematological disorders but has many complications. In retrospective studies, low gut microbiome diversity is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. In 2023, the Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1703 randomized phase 3 trial demonstrated the superiority of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) and mycophenolate mofetil to tacrolimus and methotrexate (Tac/MTX) for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis in participants with hematological malignancies undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. Here we report on the microbiome-focused companion study to 1703, Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1801, which coenrolled participants and shared trial registration. The primary endpoint was association between microbiome diversity at neutrophil engraftment and non-relapse mortality after 1 year; secondary endpoints included associations with other clinical outcomes and with baseline microbiome diversity. Based on 2575 longitudinally collected stool samples from 304 participants (Tac/MTX n = 147, PTCy n = 157), no association between engraftment microbiome diversity and non-relapse mortality was observed (P = 0.314), not meeting the primary endpoint. Lower baseline microbiome diversity was associated with shorter overall survival (P = 0.007). Safety data were reported in the original 1703 publication. In exploratory analyses, microbiome diversity and absolute microbial load were lower in PTCy compared to Tac/MTX on days 14-28 following HCT, independent of non-prophylaxis antibiotics exposure. Microbial domination events, when a single species exceeds 30% relative abundance, did not differ significantly between study arms and reflected both pathogen blooms and less severe disruptions of the microbial community. Clostridium scindens and secondary bile-acid metabolism pathways were less prevalent in PTCy than in Tac/MTX following HCT. In summary, we find prophylaxis regimens likely exert independent effects on both the microbiome and immune compartments and can also impact their interaction. Understanding whether and how microbiome-targeted interventions might improve transplant outcomes will therefore require careful disentangling of these effects within each specific treatment context. papers.abstract: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, characterized by extensive cellular and molecular heterogeneity. Here, to capture this complexity, we present LuCaS+, a multicenter single-cell RNA sequencing atlas comprising over 2.5 million nuclei from 454 clinically annotated patients with NSCLC with long-term follow-up. LuCaS+ consists of a discovery dataset (Berlin and Cologne, 364 patients) and an independent validation dataset (Munich, 90 patients). Leveraging this dataset, we identified tumor subpopulations with high metastatic potential associated with oncogenic signaling, immune evasion and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In early-stage adenocarcinoma (lung adenocarcinoma), these cells showed strong prognostic value. Integrating tumor and microenvironmental cell profiles improved survival prediction across all stages, identifying distinct tumor-immune-stromal interaction patterns. These included monocyte- and fibroblast-driven inflammation (lung adenocarcinoma), VEGF-TGFβ-mediated angiogenic feedback loops (lung squamous cell carcinoma) and immune-permissive niches promoting antitumor immunity. LuCaS+ offers a clinically anchored single-cell resource to enable personalized, biology-driven therapies in NSCLC.

papers.abstract: Diseases affect multiple cell types within tissues, but the overall landscape of the multicellular responses in human diseases remains largely unexplored. Here we categorize the multicellular responses of human diseases based on a remapped atlas of human cells, PANGEA, incorporating 12.6 million cells acquired from a pipeline that automatically processes raw sequence files from public repositories. We constructed a hierarchical cell classification framework comprising 32 major cell types and 165 cellular subtypes. On the basis of this annotation framework, we explored an extensive atlas of human cells containing 46.5 million cells from 160 diseases across 48 organs and revealed core archetypes of human diseases repeatedly found across organs. We show that this cell atlas could also serve as a reference for unbiased analysis in spatial transcriptomics, revealing spatial features associated with immunotherapy responses. Collectively, our study provides foundational resources for cell ontologies, enabling cross-tissue comparisons of cellular features in human diseases.

papers.abstract: Enfortumab vedotin (EV), an anti-nectin-4 antibody-drug conjugate, alone and with pembrolizumab (EV plus pembrolizumab [EV/P]), has transformed the treatment of locally advanced/metastatic urothelial carcinoma (la/mUC), yet remains biomarker agnostic. We prospectively evaluated [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-N188 PET/CT ([68Ga]-N188 PET/CT) as a whole-body alternative for nectin-4 imaging, with [18F]-FDG PET/CT as an active comparator and conventional computed tomography as the reference standard for staging la/mUC in 25 patients planned for EV/P. [18F]-FDG PET/CT showed a higher maximum standardized uptake value and tumor-to-background ratio than [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT across most lesion types (primary tumor, visceral, and osseous), except for lymph nodes. The overall tracer correlation was weak (Spearman r = 0.196), strongest in lymph nodes (r = 0.657), and absent in primary tumors and bone lesions. For primary tumor detection, [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT had higher specificity (86% vs 57%) and positive predictive value (92% vs 83%) than FDG, which had higher sensitivity (88% vs 67%). Nodal staging performance was similar in the tracers. For distant metastases, both achieved 100% sensitivity and negative predictive value, with [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT showing marginally higher specificity. [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT is feasible for whole-body nectin-4 assessment in la/mUC and supports a distinct biodistribution from FDG, suggesting complementary rather than interchangeable roles. Further prospective evaluation with treatment-outcome correlation is warranted before its use as a biomarker to guide EV-based therapy selection.

papers.abstract: To determine whether racial and ethnic differences in ovarian cancer survival exist across states, represented in National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, and assess whether racial and ethnic differences in ovarian cancer survival differed by factors associated with ovarian cancer prognosis. Using SEER 17 data (2000-2022), we constructed a cohort of 103,554 epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancer cases. Self-reported race was cross-classified with the NAACCR Hispanic Identification Algorithm variable to create racial and ethnic groups. Multivariable adjusted Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for ovarian cancer-specific survival by race and ethnicity, overall and stratified by registry state, histotype, stage, and treatment, adjusting for a priori covariates. Geographic heterogeneity was assessed using the I-statistic. Sensitivity analyses were restricted to high-grade serous tumors. Hispanic cases had similar ovarian cancer-specific survival, while Non-Hispanic (NH) Asian cases exhibited better ovarian cancer-specific survival than NH White cases across SEER registry states (I2 = 40.2%, p-het 0.08; I2 = 0.0%, p-het 0.52; respectively). NH Black cases generally had worse survival than NH White cases, except in Kentucky (HR: 1.01; 95%CI: 0.84-1.23) and Iowa (HR: 0.82; 95%CI: 0.55-1.22). NH Native Hawaiian/PI cases also had worse survival compared with NH White cases across SEER registry states (I2 = 0.0%; p-het 0.60). Racial and ethnic disparities in ovarian cancer-specific survival are persistent and geographically consistent, suggesting broad, multi-level determinants rather than state-specific factors underscoring the need for national efforts to ensure uniform access to high-quality healthcare.

papers.abstract: Prostate cancer affects about 1 in 8 men, with incidence influenced by age and screening. Changes in prostate-specific antigen screening recommendations have coincided with changes in stage-specific prostate cancer incidence in the United States. However, contemporary stage-specific incidence trends among men aged 40-54 years remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated temporal trends in stage-specific prostate cancer incidence among men aged 40-54 years from 2004 to 2022. A non-concurrent, population-based cohort study used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database (2004-2022). Of 86,894 men aged 40-54 years with microscopically confirmed prostate cancer, 84,554 men remained after excluding missing stage, autopsy-only reports, and death certificate-only reports. The primary exposure was year of diagnosis (continuous and eras: 2004-2011, 2012-2022, 2004-2022). The primary outcome was stage at diagnosis (localized, regional, distant). Analyses included delay-adjusted incidence rates, log-linear regression for annual percent change (APC) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), era-based comparisons, and chi-square testing. Cohort characteristics were described by age group, race/ethnicity, urbanicity, and marital status. Localized incidence significantly declined across all groups, while regional incidence significantly increased in the 45-49 (APC 3.63%; 95% CI 0.91-6.42) and 50-54 (APC 4.99%; 95% CI 3.90-6.08) age groups, and distant-stage incidence significantly increased in the 45-49 (APC 2.70%; 95% CI 2.15-3.26) and 50-54 (APC 2.93%; 95% CI 2.33-3.53) age groups. Neither regional or distant-stage incidence changed significantly among men aged 40-44 years. From 2004-2011, localized incidence significantly increased in the 45-49 group (APC 2.53%; 95% CI 0.01-5.12). From 2012-2022, localized incidence declined in the 40-44 (APC -5.58%; 95% CI -8.22 to -2.87) and 45-49 (APC -2.98%; 95% CI -5.14 to - 0.78) groups. Localized prostate cancer incidence declined while regional and distant-stage incidence increased among men aged 40-54 years. Although multiple factors may contribute to these trends, the findings support further assessment of risk-adapted screening approaches in this population.

papers.abstract: The HARVEST trial is a phase III randomized controlled trial comparing hypofractionated with conventional fractionated radiotherapy (HF-RT vs. CF-RT) with regional nodal irradiation (RNI, including internal mammary nodes [IMNs]) in breast cancer patients. In this study, we report the early toxicity profile, cosmetic outcomes and dosimetric quality assurance results. Enrolled patients were randomized into the HF-RT group (40.05 Gy/15 Fx) or CF-RT group (50 Gy/25 Fx). Acute toxicity was assessed with the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) V.3.0 scale. Cosmetic outcome was assessed using the Harvard scale. There were 400 and 401 patients enrolled in HF-RT and CF-RT group from eight centers in China, respectively. Protocol compliances exceeded 90% for most targets coverage and organs at risk constraint parameters in both groups, although IMN coverage was less complete than that of the chest wall/whole breast and supra/infraclavicular nodes. There was no significant difference of grade ≥ 2 acute toxicities between groups (RR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.52-1.22; p=0.29). Dermatitis was the most common acute toxicity, with a significantly lower rate of grade ≥ 2 events in the HF-RT group than in the CF-RT group (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.25-0.92; p=0.03). No significant differences were observed in other acute toxicities (including fatigue, pneumonitis, breast pain, dysphagia and breast edema) or in the proportion of good or excellent cosmesis among breast-conserving patients between groups. We found comparable acute toxicity and cosmesis results in HF-RT with RNI compared to CF-RT. The technical protocol was highly feasible with good protocol compliance. Additional follow-up is needed to assess the long-term efficacy and safety.

papers.abstract: While standard MRI imaging is known to underestimate glioblastoma tumor extent, advanced imaging techniques including 18-FDOPA PET, dynamic contrast enhanced (DCE) perfusion MRI, and diffusion weighted MRI (DWI) have been utilized on clinical trials to identify tumor within and beyond gadolinium enhancement for radiation targeting. This clinical trial analysis quantifies how DCE, DWI and 18-FDOPA PET identify tumor beyond standard imaging, and whether these techniques are complementary and feasible. Patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma enrolled on a phase II clinical trial underwent pre-radiation 18-FDOPA PET/CT, DCE, DWI, and standard MRI sequences. Tumor volumes were separately delineated using each imaging modality and incorporated into radiation target volumes, and were compared for overlapping and non-overlapping segments. In 153 enrolled patients included in this analysis, tumor was identified beyond conventionally used radiation volume expansions of 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20 mm from standard MRI tumor volumes in 86%, 56%, 38% and 20% of patients, respectively. Advanced imaging techniques identified partially overlapping tumor volumes; PET identified tumor outside of the advanced MRI subvolumes in 88%, while DWI and DCE identified tumor outside of standard MRI and PET in 95% cases, indicating these imaging techniques are complementary. Advanced imaging techniques including DCE, DWI, and 18-FDOPA PET allow complementary delineation of glioblastoma beyond contrast-enhancing tumor from standard MRI, and may be most valuable when used in combination. These advanced imaging methods can potentially facilitate accurate tumor targeting with reduced CTV expansions to spare normal tissue and enable safe hypofractionated radiation therapy.

papers.abstract: To compare outcome of the segment-based and gross tumor volume (GTV)-based target volume definition concepts in fractionated SBRT for vertebral metastases. This is a post hoc secondary analysis of two prospective clinical trials conducted between 2012 and 2015 (XXX1 [segment-based concept]) and between 2016 and 2023 (XXX2 [GTV-based concept]). In both trials, fractionated SBRT for painful and non-painful mechanically stable or potentially unstable vertebral metastases delivered two dose levels using simultaneous integrated boost (SIB): 35-40 Gy/5 or 48.5 Gy/10 to the high-dose planning target volume (PTV) and 20 Gy/5 and 30 Gy/10 to the conventional-dose PTV, respectively. The high-dose PTV was defined either as segment-based (XXX1) following international guidelines or GTV-based (XXX2). The primary endpoints were freedom from local progression (FFLP) and vertebral compression fracture (VCF) assessed using the Kaplan-Meier method. Patient characteristics showed several imbalances, in general more favorable for patients in the XXX2 group. The high-dose PTV in the XXX2 group (177 patients with 197 metastases) was significantly smaller than in the XXX1 group (57 patients with 63 metastases) (median 11 cm3 vs median 58 cm3, P<.001). At median follow-up of survivors of 24 months, 2-year FFLP and progressive and de novo VCF rates in the XXX2 and XXX1 groups were 95.3% vs. 86.4% (P<.001) and 10.1% vs. 34.6% (P<.001), respectively. No myelopathy or plexopathy were observed in either group. On univariable analysis the segment-based concept (Hazard ratio [HR] 5.21, 95% CI 2.53-10.72; P<.001) and lumbar spine location (HR 2.44, 95% CI 1.24-4.82, P=.01) were associated with higher rates of progressive and de novo VCF. In fractionated SBRT for vertebral metastases, reduction of the high-dose PTV to the GTV combined with focal dose escalation and low-dose elective vertebral coverage did not compromise local control and lowered the rates of VCF.

papers.abstract: Translational science is integral in deciding who would benefit the most from novel therapeutics in gynecologic oncology, yet the specimens, assays, and the data behind them are often handled inconsistently as the translational endpoints are planned late. Clinical trials involving PARP-inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), and antibody-drug conjugates in ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancer show that a biomarker can serve as an eligibility criterion, a stratification factor, a pharmacodynamic measure, or an exploratory tool. This review presents an operational framework for integrating translational science into the trial designs from the outset. We define exploratory, integrated, and integral biomarker tiers and tie each to analytical validation, clinical validation, and level of evidence. It proposes minimum standards for tissue and blood biospecimen collection, adequacy, sampling schedule depending on specimen type, pre-analytical variables, clinical annotation, and reporting with BRISQ, SPREC, and the BloodPAC technical data elements. We also cover newer techniques like ctDNA, addressing their intended use, tumor-informed versus tumor-naive assays, and sampling for minimal residual disease. We then review genomic, transcriptomic, spatial, single-cell, proteomic, metabolomic, and functional platforms, and why discovery should not be treated as validation for modern gynecologic oncology trials. Additionally, maintaining standards for data integration, reproducibility, NIH data sharing in NCI-sponsored, industry-sponsored, and institutional trials is crucial. Ultimately, adaptive master protocols and ctDNA-guided trial designs are discussed as future directions as translational endpoints deserve the same prospective planning as the primary clinical endpoint.

papers.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a prominent feature of pancreatic cancer (PDAC) and is closely associated with tumor progression and poor prognosis. However, its spatial cellular architecture and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we applied high-resolution spatial transcriptomics to construct a comprehensive atlas of the PNI microenvironment across distinct anatomical regions of intra and extra-pancreas. We observed that the Basal-like tumor subtype exhibited a higher propensity for PNI compared with the Classical subtype, a finding further supported by multiplex imaging on whole-mount histopathology. Comparative spatial analysis revealed distinct immune and stromal organization between tumor subtypes, with enrichment of M2-like macrophage potentially promoting epithelial cell migration in the vicinity of Basal-like tumors. In addition, we identified myofibroblast subset may promote Schwann cell activation and PNI-associated nerve injury was further accompanied by a shift toward inflammatory fibroblast polarization and features of CD8+ T cell exhaustion within the local microenvironment. Finally, spatial profiling indicated functional heterogeneity among tumor-associated Schwann cells, which may contribute to the tumor progression. Collectively, this study provides a spatially resolved view of the cellular and molecular landscape of PNI in PDAC and offers insights into Basal-specific neurotropic behavior and microenvironmental reorganization.

papers.abstract: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. We introduce SPIN (spatial predictive integration network), which integrates subject-specific, cell-type level, spatially informed co-expression or co-abundance networks for population-scale clinical prediction. Current implementation of SPIN includes three key modules: network construction, molecular-to-clinical prediction by Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning (BSNMani), and visualization & interpretation module. In the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) transcriptomics cohort, SPIN achieved an accuracy of 0.81 for dementia-status prediction and revealed co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance. SPIN also achieved robust survival prediction in a breast cancer single-cell proteomics cohort (C-index = 0.78), identifying two survival-associated spatial proteomic subnetworks. In summary, SPIN is an interpretable tool for spatial-omics-based clinical outcome prediction at the population scale.

papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and retrospective analyses of patient specimens identify exportin 5 (XPO5), a nuclear export receptor, as a key contributor to advanced prostate cancer (PCa) progression. Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) activates transcription of acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4). XPO5 promotes MITF nuclear export, suppresses ACSL4 transcription, and confers resistance to ferroptosis. Differential-scanning-fluorimetry-based high-throughput screening identifies 2-B8 as a molecular glue degrader of XPO5. 2-B8 covalently binds XPO5 at Cys1157 and recruits the TMEM33-RNF5 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, promoting XPO5 ubiquitination and degradation. In cellular, cell-derived xenograft, and patient-derived xenograft models, 2-B8 induces ferroptosis, suppresses tumor growth, and enhances chemosensitivity. These findings establish the XPO5-MITF-ACSL4 axis as a mechanism of ferroptosis resistance and support targeting XPO5 for the treatment of advanced PCa.

papers.abstract: Adoptive cell therapy (ACT) of tumor-specific T cells can improve survival in a subset of cancer patients. Current ACT approaches may be limited by using highly differentiated T cells, which can be inhibited by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Here, we developed an approach to optimize ACT and used spatial transcriptomics to show how stem-like and effector CD8+ T cells differentially mediate tumor control following vaccination. Spatial transcriptomic profiling of the TME showed that ACT with stem-like T cells followed by intravenous vaccination prevented immune exclusion, increased infiltration of pro-inflammatory macrophages, and reprogrammed tumor cells to upregulate type I and type II IFN signaling gene programs, which were shown to be required for tumor control. The protective transcriptomic signature of the TME in this ACT model contained overlapping biomarkers with patients who responded to ACT therapy. This approach demonstrates synergy between transferred stem-like T cells and intravenous vaccination to transcriptionally remodel the TME and enhance tumor control.
