papers.abstract: Right-sided double-lumen endobronchial tubes (DLTs) are often avoided because of technical difficulties and concerns about respiratory complications, although evidence that they increase hypoxemia during anesthesia remains limited and inconsistent. We evaluated the association between DLT side and hypoxemia during anesthesia in patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors between October 2008 and May 2023. The primary outcome was hypoxemia during anesthesia, defined as SpO2 ≤ 90% for at least 3 consecutive min during the anesthetic period. Propensity score overlap weighting was used to adjust for measured differences between patients receiving right-sided and left-sided DLTs. Odds ratios (ORs) and absolute risk differences (RDs) were estimated. Among 1,280 patients, 842 received right-sided DLTs and 438 received left-sided DLTs. After overlap weighting, measured covariates were well balanced. The incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia was 20.0% with right-sided DLTs and 18.5% with left-sided DLTs (OR, 1.10; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-1.79; P = 0.70). The RD was 1.51 percentage points (95% CI - 3.86-6.87). No clear between-group differences were observed in exploratory secondary respiratory outcomes. We found no clear evidence that right-sided DLT use was associated with a higher incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia than left-sided DLT use. However, equivalence between the two devices was not established, and further studies are needed to determine whether clinically important differences in hypoxemia risk exist.

papers.abstract: Postoperative pain management remains a critical issue in peri-operative medicine, but contemporary national data are lacking. AlgoSFAR 2 was a prospective, multicentre and observational study, conducted in randomly selected French surgical centres. Adult patients undergoing elective surgery were included. Pain was assessed at rest and during mobilization over the first three postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included postoperative opioid consumption and multimodal analgesia strategies defined as the use of at least two non-opioid strategies such as analgesics and/or regional anaesthesia. A total of 3879 patients from 80 centres were analysed. While pre-operative and immediate postoperative pain levels at rest were low, pain peaked on day 1, with high interindividual variability, and 6% of patients reported severe pain. Two thirds (66%) did not need any rescue opioids postoperatively. Overall, 95% received multimodal analgesia. These results highlight a major change in postoperative pain management in France, with broad adoption of multimodal opioid-sparing strategies. Nonetheless, a minority of patients still experience severe pain, highlighting the need for personalized management. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06487442.

papers.abstract: In severe postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), hypofibrinogenaemia is strongly associated with bleeding severity. To correct fibrinogen depletion, various fixed dosing regimens have been evaluated, but the optimal fibrinogen dosing regimen remains unknown. To date, fibrinogen pharmacokinetics have only been studied outside haemorrhagic settings (healthy or afibrinogenaemic patients) METHODS: This ancillary analysis of the TRACES trial assessed fibrinogen kinetics in 142 women with PPH > 800 ml during caesarean section, among which 31 received fibrinogen replacement. Plasma fibrinogen concentrations (n = 593) were measured using the Clauss method. A population pharmacokinetic model was developed using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. Simulations were performed to estimate loading and maintenance doses required to achieve target fibrinogen concentrations. A one-compartment logistic model adequately described plasma fibrinogen levels. Bleeding rate was identified as a key covariate to explain fibrinogen loss rate. Based on the estimated model, an optimised dosing regimen was derived to achieve and maintain predefined target fibrinogen levels. To achieve a target increase of 1 g.L-¹ in plasma fibrinogen level, the required fibrinogen loading dose is at least 2.7 g for a body weight of 50 kg. To maintain plasma fibrinogen level at a target of 2 g.L-¹ during a 1000 mL.h-¹ bleeding rate, a fibrinogen infusion rate of 0.9 g.h-¹ would be required. This work supports that an individualized target-controlled fibrinogen dosing strategy is probably required to effectively correct fibrinogen levels. Integrating such models as a clinical decision support tool into a multimodal strategy that also utilizes viscoelastic testing could optimize PPH management.

papers.abstract: A meta-analysis in a recent issue of the British Journal of Anaesthesia pools randomised evidence on intraoperative arterial blood pressure targets in nine trials in noncardiac surgery. With a total of 14 658 patients included in the analysis, the authors show that higher mean arterial pressure targets do not reduce 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, or myocardial injury. These findings reinforce the distinction between low blood pressure as a marker of perioperative vulnerability and low blood pressure as a modifiable therapeutic target. Correcting arterial pressure might normalise a number without removing the underlying physiological vulnerability that drives adverse postoperative outcomes. Therefore, this meta-analysis supports a shift from reflexive increases in blood pressure targets towards attention to the underlying cause of haemodynamic instability.

papers.abstract: Whether targeting an individualized mean arterial pressure (MAP) during cardiac surgery improves outcomes remains uncertain. The balance between improved perfusion and vasopressor-driven blood pressure augmentation is unclear. In this single-blind, multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted in 10 tertiary centers in France, adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were assigned to either individualized MAP management (target within ±10% of preoperative baseline during surgery and for 24 h postoperatively) or standard management (target MAP ≥65 mm Hg). The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, acute kidney injury, or prespecified neurologic complications within 7 days. Safety outcomes included hemorrhagic complications and transfusion requirements. A total of 172 patients were enrolled before the trial was stopped early by the data and safety monitoring board because of increased bleeding in the individualized group. Mean intraoperative MAP was higher with individualized management (80.6 vs 75.6 mm Hg; P<0.001), despite limited target adherence (33% of intraoperative time) and greater vasopressor use. The primary outcome occurred in 27 of 85 patients (32%) in the individualized group and 25 of 87 (29%) in the standard group (relative risk, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.7 to 1.8; P=0.76). Hemorrhagic complications occurred more frequently in the individualized group (18% vs 3%; P=0.003). In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, it was not possible to determine whether an individualized MAP strategy reduced major postoperative complications. More bleeding complications were observed in the individualized group. Future studies should further investigate this safety signal when evaluating individualized blood pressure targets.

papers.abstract: Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age-based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school-aged. In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0-12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre-intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5-10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0-10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound-predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size (r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW (r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator-dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school-aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under-represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed before broad implementation.

papers.abstract: Background: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) remain common after gynecological laparoscopic surgery despite guideline-based prophylaxis. Auditory information is still processed during clinically adequate general anesthesia, and operating rooms are persistently noisy, but whether attenuating intraoperative sound exposure alters PONV is unknown. Methods: In this single-center, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized trial, women aged 18 to 65 yr undergoing elective gynecological laparoscopic surgery were randomized 1:1 to wear passive noise-attenuating earmuffs from induction until the end of surgery or to usual care. All patients received dexamethasone and palonosetron. The primary outcome was PONV incidence within 48 h, defined as any episode of nausea, retching, or vomiting, assessed across three prespecified windows (post-anesthesia care unit, to 24 h, and 24 to 48 h). Secondary outcomes included PONV severity, its components, rescue antiemetic use, pain, and quality of recovery. Results: Of 364 patients assessed, 192 were randomized. PONV within 48 h occurred in 34 of 96 patients (35.4%) with noise isolation and 50 of 96 (52.1%) with control (adjusted risk difference, −0.179 [95% CI, −0.318 to −0.040]; P = 0.012). Across the three windows the overall adjusted risk difference was −0.134 (95% CI, −0.215 to −0.053; P = 0.001), with no treatment-by-window interaction ( P = 0.332); window-specific values were −0.162, −0.172, and −0.068. PONV severity, retching, and three post hoc endpoints (the vomiting-or-retching composite, complete response 72.9% versus 56.2%, and total response 64.6% versus 47.9%) favored noise isolation after false discovery rate correction. Adverse events, quality of recovery, and opioid exposure (post hoc) showed no evidence of a difference. Conclusions: Among women receiving dual antiemetic prophylaxis for gynecological laparoscopic surgery, intraoperative noise isolation was associated with a lower incidence and severity of PONV.

papers.abstract: Background: Managing postoperative pain is a complex challenge in liver surgery. Perioperative intravenous (IV) lidocaine can reduce postoperative pain, opioid use, bowel recovery time and the length of stay, in various types of surgery. Lidocaine is eliminated via hepatic metabolism, and IV lidocaine is rarely evaluated in liver surgery. This study aimed to evaluate the postoperative analgesic efficacy and safety of IV lidocaine administration in patients undergoing minor liver surgery. Methods: Patients planned for minor liver surgery were randomized 1:1 to receive either perioperative IV lidocaine, administered as a 1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 1.5 mg/kg/h until 1 hour after surgery, or placebo. All patients received postoperative opioid analgesia via a patient-controlled analgesia device. The primary outcome was postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, quality of recovery, adverse events, length of stay, and plasma lidocaine concentrations. Results: In total, 124 subjects were included. Postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery was 83 (50 – 129) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME) in the lidocaine group, and 97 (60 – 135) mg OME in the placebo group, p=0.429. Patients in the lidocaine group experienced lower pain scores at early postoperative time points, but not from postoperative day 1 onward. The Quality of recovery-40 score did not differ, and adverse events were similar between groups. In two cases, plasma concentrations of lidocaine were transiently above 5 µg/ml after bolus administration, without clinical signs of toxicity. All plasma concentrations after resection and at end of infusion were safely below toxic levels. Conclusions: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption after minor liver surgery but conferred transient early analgesic benefits and was found to be safe.

papers.abstract: We aimed to evaluate and report a protocol for video double-lumen tube (VDLT) intubation in a modified lateral position and evaluate whether it shortens in-room to cut time (IRCT; defined as the time from patient entry to incision) compared with conventional supine intubation in patients undergoing elective unilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). We conducted a single-centre, prospective, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial at a tertiary university hospital in Xi'an, China. We enrolled adults aged 18-75 yr (American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status I-III) scheduled for elective unilateral VATS requiring VDLT intubation; exclusions included body mass index > 30 kg·m-2, mouth opening < 3 cm, Mallampati class 3-4, or anticipated difficult airway. Participants were randomized 1:1 to modified-lateral-position (Group L) or supine-position (Group S) VDLT intubation using a computer-generated sequence with sealed-envelope allocation concealment. Operators were unblinded; nonoperator staff collecting postoperative data and the outcome analyst were blinded to allocation. The primary outcome was IRCT. Sixty-two patients were randomized (Group L, N = 31; Group S, N = 31), and all were analyzed for the primary outcome. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) IRCT was shorter in Group L (18.1 [2.0] min) than in Group S (31.1 [3.3] min), with a mean difference (L-S) of -13.0 min (95% confidence interval [CI], -14.4 to -11.6; P < 0.001). Intubation time was similar (mean [SD], 103 [15] sec vs 97 [15] sec; P = 0.10). Video double-lumen tube malpositioning occurred in 1/31 (3%) cases in Group L vs 15/31 (48%) cases in Group S (relative risk [RR], 0.067; 95% CI, 0.009 to 0.474; P < 0.001). Sore throat within 48 h occurred in 9/31 (29%) patients in Group L vs 18/31 (58%) patients in Group S (RR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.94; P = 0.02). In patients undergoing unilateral VATS, VDLT intubation in a modified lateral position shortened IRCT. In exploratory analyses, several secondary outcomes favoured this approach. Intubation in a modified lateral position may be a feasible alternative to conventional supine position intubation in these patients. ChiCTR.org.cn ( ChiCTR2500112254 ); first posted 21 October 2025.

papers.abstract: Nutrition is a key component of care for critically ill and surgical patients, but the organization of nutritional care and the involvement of dietitians in ICU and perioperative pathways remain variable. This survey aimed to describe respondent-reported nutritional care organization and dietitian involvement among healthcare professionals working in ICU and perioperative settings in France, with a focus on dietitian availability, clinical involvement, nutritional governance, and selected aspects of perioperative care. We conducted a voluntary cross-sectional survey among physicians and dietitians working in French ICU and perioperative settings. The survey was disseminated during the French Society of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine congress, through national professional nutrition and dietetics networks, and via social media. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Overall, 147 professionals responded, mainly ICU physicians and dietitians, and most worked in university hospitals. Among respondents, dietitian availability was reported in 67% of responses, but dedicated time was frequently limited. Involvement was mainly request-based, and participation in medical meetings or ward rounds was uncommon. A medical nutrition lead was identified in 44% of responses, a written nutrition protocol in 50%, and a task-sharing protocol allowing dietitian prescription in 9%. Reported practices suggest that dietitians are available in many French ICUs and contribute to perioperative care pathways. However, access to dietetic expertise does not necessarily translate into dedicated staffing, routine multidisciplinary participation, or structured nutritional governance. Strengthening local organization through medical leadership, written protocols, and multidisciplinary collaboration may help improve the implementation of nutritional care.

papers.abstract: Pulse contour devices estimate cardiac output (CO) from an invasive arterial blood pressure waveform. However, arterial catheters are generally used only in higher-risk patients. By contrast, automatic arm cuff devices are used for noninvasive BP monitoring in almost all hospital patients. Furthermore, these devices measure cuff pressure oscillations, which are directly related to pulsatile blood volume rather than BP. We hypothesised that automatic arm cuff devices can offer an effective means to monitor CO. A custom-built cuff device was used to measure cuff pressure and make a unique measurement of the volume of air pumped into and out of the cuff during linear deflation. Cuff device measurements, an invasive BP waveform from a radial artery catheter, and reference CO from pulmonary artery catheter bolus thermodilution were obtained during interventions from 24 liver transplant and 10 cardiac surgery patients (191 measurement sets). A basic analysis was applied to estimate CO in L min-1 as the product of heart rate, the maximum cuff pressure oscillation amplitude, the cuff-arm system compliance (derived from the cuff pressure-volume relationship), and the body-to-arm surface area ratio (derived from anthropometric information). The arm cuff-based method yielded a correlation of 0.61 (95% confidence interval 0.37-0.79) and a concordance rate of 83% (75%-91%) against the reference CO. For comparison, classic pulse contour analysis of the invasive BP waveform produced a correlation of 0.59 (0.37-0.75) and a concordance rate of 81% (72%-90%). These initial findings suggest potential for convenient CO monitoring using an automatic arm cuff device in surgical patients.

papers.abstract: To identify perioperative factors associated with the ionized-to-total magnesium (iMg/tMg) ratio at intensive care unit (ICU) admission and on postoperative day (POD) 1 after major open hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery. This single-center prospective observational study enrolled adults undergoing elective surgery. Paired iMg and tMg measurements were obtained at ICU admission and on POD 1. The primary analyses evaluated perioperative factors associated with the iMg/tMg ratio at each time point using univariable linear regression and multivariable linear regression with backward elimination. Exploratory analyses assessed temporal changes using paired t tests. Of 150 enrolled patients, 141 were analyzed. At ICU admission, the ratio was positively associated with iMg immediately after anesthesia induction (P = 0.007) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P = 0.041), and negatively associated with anesthesia time (P = 0.005) and total cholesterol (P = 0.018). On POD 1, the ratio was positively associated with intraoperative non-Mg-containing fluid volume (P = 0.016), and negatively associated with operation time (P < 0.001), hypertension (P = 0.013), and albumin (P = 0.007). Model R2 values were 0.10 and 0.20 at ICU admission and on POD 1, respectively. In exploratory analyses, the mean ratio increased between postoperative measurements (0.659 to 0.713; P < 0.001). Mean iMg decreased from 0.589 mmol/L after induction to 0.545 at ICU admission, then increased to 0.640 on POD 1 (all P < 0.001). Perioperative factors associated with the iMg/tMg ratio differed between ICU admission and POD 1 after major open hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery. Both models had limited explanatory power. These findings should be interpreted in relation to sampling time and require independent validation before informing clinical management.

papers.abstract: Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first-attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first-attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05-2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015-0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013-0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: -9.5 to -2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037-0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16-0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08-0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. Compared with SCV, ultrasound-guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

papers.abstract: Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) individualizes perioperative fluid administration according to dynamic hemodynamic variables, but its implementation remains inconsistent and its impact on patient-centered outcomes is still debated. Decision-support and automated systems have been developed to improve adherence, identify fluid responsiveness more efficiently, and reduce the workload of protocolized hemodynamic management. This structured narrative review summarizes the evidence across four outcome levels: process, surrogate hemodynamic, intermediate physiological, and patient-centered clinical. The most consistent evidence concerns process improvement: decision support increases protocol adherence and improves the proportion of fluid challenges that achieve a predefined stroke volume response, largely on non-randomized evidence. Improvements in surrogate hemodynamic control have also been reported, and selected randomized trials suggest favorable effects on microcirculatory flow and lactate. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical benefit. Fluid responsiveness does not necessarily indicate a need for fluid administration, and most available studies remain small, single-center, or focused on surrogate outcomes. Evidence that these systems improve postoperative complications, acute kidney injury, length of stay, or mortality is currently lacking. Ongoing multicenter trials should address this gap. Decision support appears to improve how perioperative fluids are administered, but whether it improves what ultimately happens to patients remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: Fractions of inspired oxygen up to 60% in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation are commonly perceived by clinicians as safe, implying a non-linear association between oxygen exposure and mortality. Also, although it seems pathophysiologically plausible that the association between oxygen exposure and mortality may depend on age, relevant evidence in adult patients is lacking. We examined whether the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality a) is non-linear and b) depends on age. We performed a secondary analysis of individual patient-level data from six acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials ("ARDSNet cohort"). We assessed linearity of the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality along with the effect of age after adjusting for covariates, including partial pressure of arterial oxygen. We tested our findings in an independent multicenter cohort. In the ARDSNet cohort involving 4953 patients with ARDS, we found that the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality was linear and independent of age (p = 0.655 for the interaction between fraction of inspired oxygen and age). In the independent cohort involving 559 patients with ARDS, we confirmed both the linearity of the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality and the lack of effect of age (p = 0.955 for the interaction). Data from the two tested multicenter cohorts suggest that the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality in ARDS may be linear and independent of age.

papers.abstract: Protein-energy malnutrition remains frequently unrecognised, under-reported, and undertreated in surgical populations despite being associated with a higher risk of postoperative complications. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic agreement between the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) operational criteria and the Subjective Global Assessment for identifying adults at risk of preoperative protein-energy malnutrition undergoing elective surgery. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 5 May 2025. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across eight included studies (n=5834) in the definitions, cut-offs, and measurement methods for GLIM phenotypic and aetiologic criteria. In six noncardiac surgical studies (n=3999), pooled sensitivity and specificity were 76% (95% confidence interval [CI] 69-81%) and 88% (95% CI 77-94%), respectively, using a random-effects bivariate model (very low certainty of evidence). Overall diagnostic agreement was fair; thus, the GLIM criteria alone may be insufficient to make the diagnosis of malnutrition and to guide nutritional interventions without additional clinical or dietetic assessment.

papers.abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB), an interventional technique that modulates sympathetic activity, has been increasingly investigated beyond traditional pain management in cardiology, neuropsychiatry, and perioperative medicine. This narrative review examines the evolving role of SGB in contemporary anesthesia practice, emphasizing that its effects may extend beyond immediate peripheral sympatholysis to longer-lasting central neural modulation. Technically, ultrasound guidance facilitates precise needle placement and low-volume injection, with improved visualization of relevant anatomy and injectate spread. Dose-finding studies have refined local-anesthetic volume and concentration, whereas continuous blockade may extend sympatholysis in selected refractory conditions. Clinically, SGB has been used in selected pain conditions, including complex regional pain syndrome and herpes zoster-related pain, and has been investigated for non-pain indications such as post-traumatic stress disorder, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and menopausal vasomotor symptoms. In perioperative settings, SGB has been evaluated for postoperative analgesia, modulation of inflammatory responses, and potential neuroprotective effects. Risk mitigation relies on real-time ultrasound visualization of the needle tip, adjacent vascular structures, and injectate spread, together with predefined management protocols for major complications. Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective studies, standardized procedural parameters, and individualized treatment pathways to support the safe, precise, and evidence-based use of SGB across clinical settings.

papers.abstract: Intraoperative hypotension is commonly defined as MAP <65 mmHg. We evaluated whether cumulative exposure across multiple MAP thresholds provides additional mortality-associated information beyond this single threshold. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults having non-cardiac, non-obstetric surgery using perioperative electronic health record data. Pressure-time burden and proportion of operative time were calculated across MAP thresholds from 50 to 150 mmHg. Decision-tree analysis using recursive partitioning sequentially grouped patients according to MAP exposure patterns associated with 30-day mortality. Discrimination of the multi-threshold blood-pressure-only model was compared with that of a model restricted to exposure below MAP 65 mmHg. Medication associations were exploratory. Among 388,407 patients, 30-day mortality was 1.49%. The multi-threshold model had greater validation discrimination than the MAP 65 mmHg model (AUROC, 0.619 vs. 0.591; ΔAUROC, 0.028; 95% CI, 0.025-0.037; p < 0.001), although the improvement was modest. Terminal exposure groups defined by complete combinations of MAP level and cumulative exposure had different observed mortality rates. Medication associations varied across groups. Observed 30-day mortality was generally higher with deeper hypotension and a greater proportion of operative time spent below MAP thresholds, although the relationship was not uniformly monotonic. Multi-threshold MAP exposure captured mortality-associated information not represented by exposure below MAP 65 mmHg alone, complementing this clinical threshold. The multi-threshold analysis identified groups with distinct pressure-time exposure patterns, providing a basis for hemodynamic profiling and investigation of hypotension-related outcomes. External validation is needed to assess the reproducibility and discrimination of these groups in other populations, followed by prospective studies to determine whether management informed by these patterns improves outcomes.

papers.abstract: Remifentanil infusion titrated to effect-site concentration (Ce) is commonly used to suppress coughing during emergence from general anesthesia; nevertheless, the optimal Ce range remains unclear. We aimed to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize the existing evidence on the optimal Ce values of remifentanil for cough suppression during emergence. We performed a comprehensive literature search using PubMed®, Embase®, Web of Science™, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar on 27 February 2025. We included prospective studies that used the up-and-down method to estimate the effective concentrations of remifentanil in 50% of patients (EC50) and 95% of patients (EC95) for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia with tracheal intubation in adult patients. We excluded studies in children or patients undergoing cardiac surgery, as well as those that only compared predefined Ce targets of remifentanil to determine optimal dosing. We obtained pooled estimates using a random-effects model with inverse-variance method, and heterogeneity was quantified using the I2 statistic. We assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool for randomized trials and the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies for nonrandomized comparative or single-arm studies. The primary outcome was EC50 estimated using the up-and-down method, with secondary outcomes including model-based EC50 and EC95 estimates. We included 22 prospective studies comprising 857 adult participants, and none were assessed as being at a high risk of bias or of low methodologic quality. Based on 28 groups and 653 participants across 17 studies, the pooled mean EC50 from the up-and-down method was 2.0 ng·mL-1 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.8 to 2.3), with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 74.5%). Based on 29 groups and 693 participants across 18 studies, the model-based EC50 was 1.9 ng·mL-1 (95% CI, 1.6 to 2.1), with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 96.1%). Based on 31 groups and 809 participants across 20 studies, the model-based EC95 was 2.7 ng·mL-1 (95% CI, 2.5 to 3.0), with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 99.5%). Subgroup analyses revealed higher mean EC50 values in male individuals (2.6 ng·mL-1) and the highest mean EC50 in patients undergoing video-assisted thoracic surgery (2.6 ng·mL-1). Using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation framework, the certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all outcomes. The identified EC50 and EC95 values of remifentanil for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia in adults were 2.0 and 2.7 ng·mL-1, respectively. Patient sex and surgical type may influence the required Ce. Careful dose adjustment is recommended to avoid delayed awakening and hypoventilation, especially in cases requiring higher concentrations. papers.abstract: Inhaled anesthetic use contributes to environmental harm through release of potent greenhouse gases (GHG). Emissions can be reduced with the use of safe practice changes, including avoidance of high impact agents like desflurane and nitrous oxide, use of low fresh gas flows, and adoption of total intravenous and regional anesthesia when clinically appropriate. These evidence-based practices have been recommended for years, but actual practice changes have not been widely adopted. The Project SPRUCE (Saving our Planet by Reducing Carbon Emissions) consortium brought together twelve pediatric anesthesia groups into a partnership working to reduce GHG emissions from pediatric anesthesia care. The consortium implemented quality improvement strategies, including change management methods, to reduce GHG emissions from inhaled anesthetics by at least 50%. Change management and quality improvement strategies were utilized to disseminate strategies, implement emissions reduction techniques, and track emissions in pediatric anesthesia care. Specific interventions included education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams. The consortium facilitated adoption of practice changes among anesthesia groups, and sustained emissions reductions though shifts in culture. Greenhouse gas emissions from inhaled anesthesia decreased by 63% (range 43-91%) During the study period, the incidence of nitrous oxide use was reduced by 62.4%, and the average volume of nitrous oxide used per case decreased by 83.5%. Project SPRUCE prevented a total of 14,381 metric tons of excess carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions from inhaled anesthetics. Collaborative action within our consortium supported widespread and significant reductions in harmful greenhouse gas emissions from pediatric anesthesia care through education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams.

papers.abstract: Reversal of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) is a routine component of general anaesthesia with important implications for recovery quality and peri-operative safety. Recent changes in the cost of sugammadex, together with its efficacy and adverse effect profile relative to neostigmine, may influence its broader clinical use. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of sugammadex compared with neostigmine in adult patients. Systematic review of randomised controlled trials with meta-analyses and trial sequential analyses. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. This is an update of a 2017 Cochrane review. Online databases were searched up to December 2025. Randomised trials enrolling adults receiving rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures and comparing sugammadex with neostigmine were included. The outcomes included NMB recovery time and risk of various adverse events. We included 165 trials with 19 124 participants. Risk of bias was generally unclear or high. NMB monitoring technique was reported in 113 trials, mostly acceleromyography. Time to reversal of NMB from second twitch to a train-of-four ratio more than 0.9 was shorter with sugammadex 2 mg kg-1 versus neostigmine 0.05 mg kg-1 (mean difference = -10.49 min (95% confidence interval, -11.90 to -9.08), GRADE: moderate). Sugammadex probably reduces the number of patients with at least one adverse event compared with neostigmine (risk ratio = 0.72 (95% confidence interval, 0.61 to 0.84), GRADE: moderate). When looking at specific adverse events, sugammadex probably reduces the risk of residual NMB, inadequate NMB reversal, desaturation, atelectasis, increased upper airway secretion, airway obstruction, bradycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention (GRADE: moderate). Sugammadex probably reverses NMB more rapidly and with fewer adverse events than neostigmine. Broader use of sugammadex has the potential to improve peri-operative outcomes.

papers.abstract: Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia is generally considered to follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. In a recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, Aboelsaod and colleagues integrate national epidemiological data, anaesthetic exposure histories, population genomics, contracture test phenotyping, and Bayesian modelling to estimate the prevalence of individuals capable of developing clinical malignant hyperthermia. Their findings support a threshold model in which variants contribute different degrees of biological liability, potentially modified by other genetic and environmental factors, whereas the probability of reacting during a triggering exposure seems relatively similar once an individual has crossed this threshold. The study also illustrates how combining complementary sources of imperfect evidence can improve risk estimation for rare, exposure-dependent disorders. Ultimately, malignant hyperthermia genetics needs to move beyond categorical variant classification towards variant-specific penetrance estimates that incorporate genetic background, ancestry, exposure history, and other determinants of clinical expression.

papers.abstract: We aimed to assess the public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related hospital care tasks in Japan and examine associated factors. We conducted a cross-sectional, nationwide, quota-based web survey of adults in Japan in July 2025. Of the 1,944 respondents who initiated the survey, 1,844 completed (94.9%) it, and 1,000 responses were analyzed after quota completion (ages 20-69 yr). The outcomes were attribution (yes/no) of four anesthesia-related hospital care tasks to anesthesiologists: intraoperative anesthesia, postoperative pain management, procedural sedation/analgesia (PSA), and labour neuraxial analgesia (LNA). For each outcome, we fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, the Health Interest Scale (HIS), Communicative and Critical Health Literacy (CCHL), board-certified anesthesiologist density, information sources, and task-matched experience, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) control. Attribution was highest for intraoperative anesthesia (84.7%), followed by LNA (65.2%), PSA (37.4%), and postoperative pain management (13.5%). After FDR control, university education or higher was associated with greater attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.30 to 3.32), PSA (aOR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.15 to 2.30), and LNA (aOR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.30 to 2.55). Task-matched prior experience attributed to anesthesiologists was associated with higher attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (aOR, 3.75; 95% CI, 1.76 to 8.80) and PSA (aOR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.34 to 4.43). Fictional media was the only information-source factor that remained significant after FDR control (intraoperative anesthesia: aOR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.79 to 4.25; PSA: aOR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.42 to 2.56). No factor met the FDR threshold for postoperative pain management. HIS, CCHL, and anesthesiologist density showed no consistent adjusted associations. Public attribution of anesthesiologists' roles in Japan varied by task. Educational attainment, task-matched experience, and information sources were more consistently associated with attribution than general health traits or workforce context, supporting the value of role-explicit, task-specific communication strategies.

papers.abstract: Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique.

papers.abstract: The Delphi methodology is a widely-used tool for achieving expert consensus in healthcare, particularly in areas where empirical evidence is limited or uncertain. Despite its structured design, the Delphi process remains vulnerable to implicit cognitive biases that may influence judgement and group decision-making. Such biases may inadvertently affect the quality of the consensus process, allow louder voices to influence outcomes, restrict inclusivity and undermine the validity, transparency and evidence-based nature of recommendations. We conducted a methodological review synthesising literature from cognitive psychology, behavioural science and methodological research on consensus development and Delphi processes. Using a concept-mapping approach, established cognitive biases were mapped to different stages of the Delphi process, including study design; panel selection; survey development; iterative scoring; and consensus interpretation. Ten cognitive biases were organised into four domains reflecting different levels of influence within consensus development: steering-group and design-level biases, panel composition and contextual biases, social influence and conformity biases; and individual cognitive heuristic biases. A conceptual framework was developed to systematically identify these biases within Delphi-based consensus studies. Examples illustrating how these biases may arise in healthcare Delphi processes are presented, alongside potential mitigation strategies. Recognition and mitigation of cognitive biases are essential for strengthening the methodological rigour and credibility of Delphi studies. Strategies to reduce bias include diversifying expert panels; using neutral language in survey statements; maintaining anonymity during voting; involving methodological expertise in Delphi design; and ensuring transparent iterative feedback. The framework needs prospective validation before its widespread use and may assist journal editors and peer reviewers in critically appraising Delphi studies and improving reporting standards in consensus research.

papers.abstract: Readmission after discharge from the intensive care unit (ICU) occurs globally at a rate of approximately 1-12% and is associated with adverse patient outcomes. Despite these findings, there is no internationally accepted tool to guide or standardize decisions regarding ICU discharge. In this scoping review, we aimed to evaluate the use of early warning scores (EWSs) measured at or around the time of ICU discharge as predictors of subsequent ICU readmission in adult and pediatric populations. With support from a medical librarian, we searched MEDLINE®, Embase®, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature from database inception to December 14, 2025. We included quantitative observational and interventional studies that evaluated any EWS (e.g., National EWS [NEWS]/NEWS2, Modified EWS [MEWS], Pediatric EWS [PEWS], Rothman Index, Risk Scoring Index, or related tools) at ICU discharge, immediately prior to transfer, or immediately upon ward admission and reported unplanned ICU readmission following transfer to a hospital ward. Unplanned ICU readmissions were defined as any unplanned return to an ICU after discharge to the ward. We excluded studies in which patients were discharged to locations other than a ward (e.g., home, long-term care) or that focused solely on interfacility transfer. Screening and data extraction were performed in duplicate using a standardized template, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The search identified 7,977 records, of which 4,824 remained after removal of duplicates. Of the articles, 58 underwent full-text review, and 20 studies met inclusion criteria. The studies were conducted across North America, Europe, and Asia and included both adult (n = 14) and pediatric (n = 6) populations. All were observational (retrospective or prospective) or pre-post intervention designs; no randomized controlled trials were identified. A range of tools were evaluated, including NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS, PEWS, the Rothman Index, the Risk Scoring Index, and several machine-learning-based EWS models. Of the 20 studies, 17 reported a significant association between higher EWS values at or near ICU discharge and increased risk of unplanned ICU readmission, while three found no significant association. Across studies, readmission rates and EWS thresholds varied, and there was considerable heterogeneity in populations, settings, and outcome time frames. The risk of bias was generally low to moderate across QUADAS-2 domains, although several studies had high or unclear risk in key areas-most commonly patient selection and index test blinding-limiting causal inference. Most available studies report that higher EWS values at ICU discharge are associated with an increased likelihood of ICU readmission. Early warning scores may therefore serve as useful adjuncts to clinical judgement when assessing discharge readiness. Nevertheless, the current evidence base is limited by the absence of randomized or robust interventional trials, and substantial heterogeneity, which limits causal inference and the ability to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve outcomes. Further multicentre prospective studies are needed to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve patient outcomes, reduce readmissions, and optimize use of ICU resources.

papers.abstract: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

papers.abstract: Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is a clinically important postoperative complication, particularly in patients at high risk for voiding dysfunction. Sugammadex reverses aminosteroid neuromuscular blockade without requiring concomitant antimuscarinic administration and may therefore reduce the risk of POUR compared with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate. In this prospective randomised trial, 124 adults at high risk for POUR undergoing elective otolaryngologic surgery were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive neostigmine-glycopyrrolate or sugammadex for neuromuscular block reversal. The primary outcome was confirmed POUR, defined as inability to void requiring urinary catheterisation with an ultrasound-confirmed bladder volume ≥400 mL. Secondary outcomes included postoperative nausea and vomiting, haemodynamic events, patient-reported thirst intensity, and hospital length of stay. Confirmed POUR occurred in 12 of 62 patients (19.4%) in the neostigmine-glycopyrrolate group and in none of the 62 patients (0%) in the sugammadex group (risk difference, 19.4%; 95% CI, 9.5%-30.9%; P < 0.001; NNT = 6). Exploratory analysis showed that symptomatic urinary retention was also more frequent with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate than with sugammadex (40.3% vs. 4.8%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in postoperative nausea and vomiting, haemodynamic events, thirst intensity, or hospital length of stay; secondary-outcome comparisons were not powered to detect between-group differences. Among patients at high risk for POUR undergoing elective otolaryngologic surgery, sugammadex reduced the risk of confirmed POUR compared with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate. Comparisons of secondary outcomes were underpowered and should be interpreted cautiously. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06398899; principal investigator: Pei-Lin Lin; registered on 5 March 2024).
